results.summary_before: This is a 4-point, 8-bit fixed-point Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) engine implemented in SystemVerilog. It uses a radix-2 decimation-in-time architecture with butterfly modules and twiddle factor multiplication to compute the frequency-domain representation of four complex samples. The design interfaces with switches for control, a bidirectional data bus for samples and results, and a single-digit 7-segment display for status. External hardware includes a 7-segment display, switches, and a reset button.

results.summary_before: This Verilog design implements a 4-bit ALU slice intended for mini and microcomputer CPUs, supporting ADD, AND, OR, XOR, pass-through, and shift operations selected by a 3-bit function code. It provides carry in/out, complement, zero, and negative-zero flags, and was tested on an Intel/Altera FPGA. The design is controlled entirely through its input pins and requires no external hardware beyond the FPGA used for verification. It is a straightforward educational ALU block with clear function and pin documentation.

results.summary_before: This is a bit-serial implementation of a subset of the PDP-8 computer, adapted from a textbook example and using one-hot state encoding generated by VITO. It emulates instructions such as AND, TAD, ISZ, DCA, JMP, and microinstructions, with a reduced memory of 128 words accessed serially. The design requires an external serial memory emulation, typically via a Python testbench, and includes wait states to accommodate cocotb testing. It is an educational project demonstrating computer architecture and hardware design.

results.summary_before: This design models a Quadratic Integrate and Fire (QIF) neuron using stochastic computing in bipolar format. It uses an LFSR to generate random bitstreams and implements the neuron equation with XNOR, MUX, and up/down counter. The design is tested by setting a 9-bit input value and observing the neuron's current value on the outputs. It requires an oscilloscope to view the output.

results.summary_before: This project implements a finite state machine (FSM) combined with a counter to simulate a traffic light controller for two perpendicular streets. It was developed as part of the Digital Systems course at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile. The design supports normal mode with priority for Street A and a parade mode where Street B stays green indefinitely. It requires external LEDs and push-buttons for testing and can be simulated using cocotb.
